subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on the roles and functions of education, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain the roles and functions of education for GCSE Sociology simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Formal and informal education: the official and hidden curriculum
The functionalist view of the roles and functions of education
The Marxist view of the roles and functions of education
The feminist view of the roles and functions of education
Explanations for differences in educational achievement by social class
Explanations for differences in educational achievement by ethnicity
Explanations for differences in educational achievement by gender
In-school factors: labelling, sub-cultures and the self-fulfilling prophecy

questions.lo: Formal and informal education: the official and hidden curriculum
questions.q: Which of the following best describes the 'hidden curriculum'?
options: The timetable of lessons published at the start of term
The list of examinable subjects printed in a school prospectus
The norms, values and expectations pupils learn informally, such as punctuality and conformity
Private tuition arranged outside normal school hours
questions.explain: The hidden curriculum refers to the things pupils learn informally at school, such as obedience, punctuality, conformity and gender roles, rather than the formal subject content of the official curriculum.

questions.lo: Formal and informal education: the official and hidden curriculum
questions.q: A school requires pupils to line up silently, wear uniform and address teachers formally. These rules are an example of the school transmitting values through the:
options: Vocational curriculum
Hidden curriculum
Examination syllabus
Official curriculum
questions.explain: Rules about uniform, silence and deference are not part of the taught subject content. They teach conformity and respect for authority informally, which is the hidden curriculum.

questions.lo: The functionalist view of the roles and functions of education
questions.q: According to the functionalist view, one key role of education is 'role allocation'. This means education:
options: Reproduces the ruling-class ideology of capitalism
Sifts and sorts people into the jobs best suited to their abilities
Removes the need for examinations
Teaches only working-class pupils to fail
questions.explain: Functionalists such as Parsons and Davis and Moore argue education sifts and sorts pupils by ability (role allocation), matching the most talented to the most important roles in a meritocratic society.

questions.lo: The functionalist view of the roles and functions of education
questions.q: Functionalists argue that education promotes 'value consensus'. This means education:
options: Encourages pupils to reject authority
Prevents social mobility
Passes on shared norms and values that bind society together
Benefits only the bourgeoisie
questions.explain: Functionalists see education as an agency of secondary socialisation that transmits society's shared values, creating value consensus and social cohesion (Durkheim's idea of a 'society in miniature').

questions.lo: The functionalist view of the roles and functions of education
questions.q: Which criticism is most often made of the functionalist view of education?
options: It claims education has no economic function
It argues that all pupils fail equally
It assumes education is truly meritocratic and overlooks how inequality shapes achievement
It ignores the fact that schools socialise pupils at all
questions.explain: A key limitation is that functionalism assumes education is meritocratic. Critics argue it ignores how class, gender and ethnicity inequalities affect achievement, so success is not simply based on ability and effort.

questions.lo: The Marxist view of the roles and functions of education
questions.q: Marxists argue that education spreads the 'myth of meritocracy'. This means education:
options: Abolishes social class differences
Makes people wrongly believe success is based on merit, disguising class inequality
Guarantees every pupil an equal chance of success
Rewards only the hardest-working pupils regardless of background
questions.explain: For Marxists, meritocracy is a myth: education makes failure look like the fault of the individual rather than the result of an unequal system, which legitimises and reproduces class inequality.

questions.lo: The Marxist view of the roles and functions of education
questions.q: The concept of 'cultural capital', used to explain why middle-class pupils tend to do better, refers to:
options: The number of books printed each year
The knowledge, language and cultural attitudes valued by schools that middle-class children tend to possess
The money parents spend on private tutors
Government spending on state schools
questions.explain: Cultural capital (associated with Bourdieu) is the language, knowledge and cultural attitudes of the middle class. Because schools reward this culture, middle-class pupils have an advantage over working-class pupils.

questions.lo: The Marxist view of the roles and functions of education
questions.q: A Marxist would argue that the hidden curriculum in schools mainly prepares working-class pupils to:
options: Accept a future as obedient, conformist workers for capitalism
Reject all forms of authority
Become powerful business owners
Achieve rapid upward social mobility
questions.explain: Marxists such as Bowles and Gintis argue the hidden curriculum produces an obedient, docile workforce. Schooling 'corresponds' to the workplace, reproducing the labour capitalism needs.

questions.lo: The feminist view of the roles and functions of education
questions.q: The feminist view of education argues that schools often:
options: Have completely removed all gender differences
Treat boys and girls in an identical, neutral way
Reinforce patriarchal values and channel girls and boys towards gendered subjects and roles
Only benefit girls at the expense of boys
questions.explain: Feminists argue education can reproduce patriarchy through a gendered curriculum, teacher expectations and subject 'choices', channelling girls and boys towards traditional gender roles.

questions.lo: The feminist view of the roles and functions of education
questions.q: A feminist sociologist notices that girls are steered towards subjects like textiles and boys towards engineering. This is best described as:
options: Value consensus
The correspondence principle
Compensatory education
The gendered curriculum and gendered subject choice
questions.explain: When subjects become associated with one gender and pupils are channelled accordingly, feminists call this a gendered curriculum / gendered subject choice, which can reproduce wider gender inequality.

questions.lo: Explanations for differences in educational achievement by social class
questions.q: Which of the following is a MATERIAL factor used to explain lower achievement among some working-class pupils?
options: A restricted linguistic code
Teacher labelling
An anti-school subculture
Lack of a quiet study space, books or access to digital technology at home
questions.explain: Material factors are to do with money and physical resources, such as housing, study space, books and access to digital technology. Labelling, language and subcultures are cultural or in-school factors.

questions.lo: Explanations for differences in educational achievement by social class
questions.q: 'Compensatory education' policies (such as extra funding or early-years programmes) are designed to:
options: Increase class sizes in deprived areas
Remove examinations for working-class pupils
Make up for disadvantages faced by children from poorer backgrounds
Reward pupils who already achieve highly
questions.explain: Compensatory education aims to compensate for material and cultural deprivation by giving extra resources or support to disadvantaged pupils, so they can compete on more equal terms.

questions.lo: Explanations for differences in educational achievement by ethnicity
questions.q: An 'ethnocentric curriculum' is one that:
options: Removes all history from the syllabus
Reflects and prioritises the culture and viewpoint of one dominant ethnic group
Is taught only in minority languages
Treats all cultures equally
questions.explain: An ethnocentric curriculum privileges the culture, history and language of the dominant ethnic group, which can disadvantage and alienate pupils from minority ethnic backgrounds.

questions.lo: Explanations for differences in educational achievement by ethnicity
questions.q: Which factor is an IN-SCHOOL explanation for ethnic differences in achievement?
options: Family income and housing quality
The national birth rate
Teacher labelling and institutional racism within the school
Parents' occupation
questions.explain: In-school factors happen inside education, such as teacher labelling, an ethnocentric curriculum and institutional racism. Income, housing and occupation are out-of-school (home) factors.

questions.lo: Explanations for differences in educational achievement by gender
questions.q: One reason often given for girls' improved achievement in recent decades is:
options: The abolition of all coursework
The removal of girls from science subjects
A fall in the number of female teachers
Changes in female expectations and ambitions linked to greater equality and employment opportunities
questions.explain: Sociologists link girls' rising achievement to changing gender roles, higher ambitions and expanded opportunities for women in work, alongside changes such as the girl-friendly nature of some assessment.

questions.lo: In-school factors: labelling, sub-cultures and the self-fulfilling prophecy
questions.q: The 'self-fulfilling prophecy' in education occurs when:
options: Examinations are marked by computers
Schools ignore all differences between pupils
Pupils choose their own subjects freely
A teacher's label leads a pupil to behave in line with that label, making it come true
questions.explain: A self-fulfilling prophecy happens when a teacher labels a pupil (e.g. as 'bright' or 'a troublemaker'), the pupil internalises the label, and their behaviour and achievement come to match it.

questions.lo: In-school factors: labelling, sub-cultures and the self-fulfilling prophecy
questions.q: A group of pupils placed in the bottom set reject the value of school, disrupt lessons and gain status by misbehaving. Sociologists call this:
options: An anti-school subculture
A pro-school subculture
Meritocracy
Value consensus
questions.explain: An anti-school (counter-school) subculture forms when pupils denied status in school gain it by opposing school values. It is often linked to streaming/setting and negative labelling.

questions.lo: In-school factors: labelling, sub-cultures and the self-fulfilling prophecy
questions.q: Dividing pupils into different ability groups or classes, which can trigger labelling and subcultures, is known as:
options: Cultural capital
Vocationalism
Setting or streaming by ability
Compensatory education
questions.explain: Setting and streaming group pupils by ability. Critics argue this can lead to lower sets being negatively labelled, forming anti-school subcultures and experiencing a self-fulfilling prophecy of failure.

questions.lo: Education, meritocracy and social mobility
questions.q: A 'meritocracy' is a society in which rewards and positions are allocated on the basis of:
options: Family wealth and inheritance
Ability and effort
Ethnic background
Gender
questions.explain: In a meritocracy, success is based on ability and effort rather than ascribed characteristics such as class, wealth, gender or ethnicity. Functionalists believe education promotes this; Marxists say it is a myth.

questions.lo: Education, meritocracy and social mobility
questions.q: Which statement best captures the disagreement between functionalists and Marxists about education and social mobility?
options: Both agree education always guarantees upward mobility for everyone
Marxists believe education creates perfect equality, functionalists disagree
Neither theory thinks education affects mobility at all
Functionalists see education as opening up fair opportunities for mobility, while Marxists argue it mostly reproduces existing class inequalities
questions.explain: Functionalists view education as a meritocratic ladder enabling social mobility. Marxists argue it reproduces class inequality across generations, so genuine mobility is limited and the myth of meritocracy hides this.
